newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian gasoline producers' losses here to stay.
newsitem.headline: Asian gasoline producers' losses here to stay.

text.p: Asian gasoline producers are likely to face price pressure over the next ten years as the region heads into a glut of gasoline, but a growing deficit of naphtha, dampening investment in building new reformers, industry sources said.

Growing refinery capacity in Asia will switch the region's gasoline deficit of 44,000 barresl per day (bpd) in 1994 to a surplus of 75,000 bpd in 1997, figures from the Hawaii-based research group East-West Center show.
The figures forecast that the gasoline surplus will peak in 1998 at 107,000 bpd, but will still be 82,000 bpd by 2005.
New refining capacity in Thailand and South Korea has already pushed the region into excess supply since the middle of the year and has started exerting pressure on prices.
China's new 100,000 barrel-per-day (bpd) Dalian refinery, which started operations in October, is the latest entry into the gasoline export market, emerging to offer a November cargo.

As a result, refiners' profits have crumbled, particularly in reforming -- a secondary process to convert low octane straight-run naphtha into high octane gasoline -- blending component reformate, producing hydrogen as a by-product.
"The naphtha-mogas (gasoline) spread is definitely below $3 (a barrel) which is our breakeven costs," said a Singapore refinery planning manager, referring to the profit margin from reformers.
"But refiners have very little choice. They have to run their reformers for the hydrogen," he said. "You could say the reformer is now more of a hydrogen processor."

Singapore refiners said they have little flexibility to shutdown or cut runs of the reformer due to strong demand for hydrogen which is used for either hydrodesulphurising or hydrocracking to produce cleaner oil products.
And demand for cleaner products is rising as Asia moves towards greener fuels.

"Many times it is not worthwhile to buy the high aromatic naphtha. The price you pay for the feedstock naphtha is higher than the mogas," said a senior official from Taiwan's Chinese Petroleum Corp (CPC), one of Asia's regular importers of gasoline.
CPC is however in the initial stages of planning to build a continous catalyst regenerator (CCR), or reformer, which would produce reformate.
"But from the perspective of the refiners, there is a different view point," the official said. "The only way to achieve environmental change is through a new CCR."
Taiwan has a mandate to reduce the benzene content in gasoline from three percent to one percent by 2000.
Meanwhile, strong petrochemical demand with new plants coming onstream in Thailand, Singapore, Indonesia and India will prompt regional naphtha imports for years to come, industry sources said.
East-West Center projects naphtha's deficit in 1994 at 417,000 bpd, growing to 488,000 bpd by 1997 and 516,000 bpd in 2000. By 2005, it is expected to drop to 490,000 bpd.
Sources in Singapore, Asia's major swing refined products exporter, said refiners are holding back on reforming capacity expansion plans because of the expectation of tight margins for several years.
Unless the naphtha-mogas spread widens beyond the $3 per barrel long term, reforming units will be unable to pay for themselves.

"I don't think anybody will be too excited to build reformers unless they are connected to petrochemical complex where intergrated economics can work," said a logistics planning manager at a refinery in Singapore.
"There is no new investment (in reformers) until 2000 when (gasoline) demand picks up," said a refinery planning manager. "It is very difficult to justify a new reformer."
--Singapore newsroom (+65-870-3086)
